titre: A Song Lasts Three Minutes Because of a Groove That Disappeared
accroche: In 1974, Billy Joel sings about how his hit was cut short for radio. His record company ends up cutting the song itself short.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1974, Billy Joel releases *The Entertainer*, a song that tells, with irony, how his previous hit, *Piano Man*, was cut from five minutes forty seconds to three minutes five seconds to fit commercial radio. The irony closes in on itself: his record company in turn shortens the single version of *The Entertainer*, from three minutes forty-one seconds to three minutes eleven seconds, by cutting an entire verse. That length is not arbitrary. It comes from a technology that Billy Joel, in 1974, had long since stopped using.

## A Groove With a Fixed Length

Since the beginning of the 20th century, the industry standard has been the 78 rpm record: a shellac disc cut with a single spiral groove, read by a needle turning at 78 revolutions per minute. The width of that groove, set by the size of the needle, determines both the fidelity of the sound and the total length of the spiral that can be cut on a ten-inch disc: about three minutes of music per side, a little more on a twelve-inch disc. Beyond that threshold, there are only two options: cut the work, or spread it over several discs that have to be changed in the middle of listening.

Composers adapt, sometimes to the point of irony. In 1925, Igor Stravinsky writes his *Sérénade en la* (Serenade in A) for piano, four movements each calibrated to fill exactly one side of a ten-inch 78: the technical constraint becomes a compositional principle. Edward Elgar, for his part, cuts his violin concerto from about fifty minutes to about twenty in order to record it. The musicologist Mark Katz, of the University of North Carolina, notes that even jazz in the studio disciplines itself: Louis Armstrong writes out *Cornet Chop Suey* in musical notation two years before recording it, to make sure his improvisations fit in the time allotted.

## What It Shifts

The 78 rpm record disappears in the 1950s, replaced by the long-playing record and then by media that no longer impose any physical limit on duration. The three-minute song does not disappear: it becomes a convention, taken up by radio and then by the music video, all the way to the algorithms of streaming platforms, which today favor short tracks because a track listened to the end counts for more than one interrupted partway through. The material constraint has been gone for seventy years; the form it imposed keeps imposing itself, for economic reasons that have nothing to do with the width of a groove.

citation.texte: He was asked by a record company to write a piece, and he decided to write a four-movement piece for a piano, which he called "Serenade in A," and he decided to write it so that each movement lasted exactly the length of a 10-inch 78-RPM record.

carte.punch: The record that limited songs to about three minutes disappeared in the 1950s.
carte.idee: The ten-inch 78 rpm record could hold only about three minutes of music per side, because of the width of its groove. Stravinsky even calibrated his Serenade in A to that limit in 1925. The medium was replaced by the long-playing record, but the three-minute song remained a convention.

quiz.question: Why did 78 rpm records limit a song to about three minutes?
choix: Because an official regulation limited the length of commercial recordings
Because the width of the groove, set by the size of the needle, limited the length of the spiral that could be cut
Because the shellac of the disc cracked beyond three minutes of continuous cutting
Because recording studios billed each session by the minute
quiz.explication: The width of the groove, determined by the size of the needle used to cut it, sets the total length of the spiral that can be inscribed on a ten-inch disc turning at 78 revolutions per minute, about three minutes per side. It is neither a legal rule, nor a fragility of the material, nor a studio rate: the limit is purely geometric.
